installation.note: umount is a built-in command available on all Linux systems by default

overview.summary: The umount command detaches a filesystem from the directory tree, making it safe to remove the device. It's essential for safely ejecting USB drives, external storage, and network filesystems.
when_to_use: Safely remove USB drives or external storage
Free up mount points for remounting

syntax.description: Unmount a filesystem by specifying either the mount point directory or the device. The filesystem must not be in use.

options.description: Unmount all filesystems mentioned in /etc/mtab (except root)
options.use_case: Unmount all non-essential filesystems, typically during shutdown

options.description: Unmount all mountpoints for the given filesystem
options.use_case: Unmount a device from all mount points if mounted multiple times

options.description: If the unmounted device was a loop device, also free this loop device
options.use_case: When unmounting ISO images or loop devices

options.description: Force unmount (in case of an unreachable NFS system)
options.use_case: When network filesystem is unreachable and normal unmount fails

options.description: Lazy unmount - detach the filesystem now, clean up later
options.use_case: When device is busy but you need to unmount immediately (use with caution)

options.description: If unmounting fails, try to remount read-only
options.use_case: When normal unmount fails, attempt read-only remount as fallback
To see detailed information about the unmount operation

misconceptions.title: Unmounting is optional
misconceptions.misconception: You can safely remove USB drives without unmounting
misconceptions.reality: Always unmount before removing storage devices. Failure to unmount can cause data loss, filesystem corruption, or both. The system buffers writes, and unmount ensures all data is written.
misconceptions.tip: Make it a habit: always umount before physically removing devices

misconceptions.title: Unmount deletes files
misconceptions.misconception: Unmounting removes files from the device
misconceptions.reality: Unmount only detaches the filesystem from the directory tree. All files remain on the device. You can remount it later and access all files.
misconceptions.tip: Unmount is safe - it only makes the filesystem inaccessible, not deleted

common_pitfalls.description: Cannot unmount because files or directories are in use
common_pitfalls.solution: Close all files, exit all directories on the mount point. Use lsof /mnt/usb to find processes using it, or use umount -l for lazy unmount

common_pitfalls.description: Regular users cannot unmount most filesystems
common_pitfalls.solution: Use sudo for unmounting. Some filesystems mounted by users can be unmounted by the same user

common_pitfalls.description: Trying to unmount something that isn't mounted
common_pitfalls.solution: Check mounted filesystems with mount or df to verify the mount point exists

related_commands.description: Mount filesystems that are unmounted with umount

best_practices: Always unmount before physically removing storage devices
Check for active processes with lsof before unmounting if you get 'device busy' errors
Use umount -v for confirmation of successful unmount
Close all terminal windows and file managers that might be accessing the mount point
Wait for unmount to complete before removing the device
performance_tips: Unmounting is usually very fast unless the device is busy
Lazy unmount (-l) can help when you need immediate unmount but processes are still using files
Unmount network filesystems when not in use to free network resources

additional_notes.safety: Unmounting ensures all buffered writes are flushed to the device
additional_notes.auto_unmount: Some desktop environments auto-unmount USB devices when you click 'Eject'
additional_notes.remount: You can remount a filesystem after unmounting - all files will still be there
additional_notes.critical: Never force-remove a device without unmounting - this can cause permanent data loss
